body:
Thank you all for attending the meeting today and a special thank you to Mason for taking meeting notes! Here are the notes from this meeting (the next one is at https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11170):

### Agenda  
Attendees: Stephen Chenney, Dominic Farolino, Dan Clark, Mason Freed, Benjamin VanderSloot, Emilio Cobos Álvarez, Panos Astithas, Di Zhang, Noam Rosenthal, Keith Cirkel, Rakesh Goulikar, Joey Arhar, Luke Warlow, Chris Wilson, Brian Kardell, Simon Pieters  
Scribe: Mason

1. Review past action items
    1.  Olli and Anne will take a look at [ARIA notify iframe restrictions](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11004).
        1. [smaug] not done. 
    1. Chris will talk to the CSSWG about [native/primitive appearance of Customizable `<select>`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11107).
        1. Not done as far as we can tell.
    1. Olli will review the [Update dialog to minimally handle open attribute mutations](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10954).
        1. [smaug] not done
1. Carryovers from last time
    1. [Di] [Naming of Composed Range](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/issues/1363)
        1. Consensus in the room is to use "composed range" and "legacy uncomposed range".
    1. [Dom] [FACE reset algorithm during custom element creation](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11122)
        1. [https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11122#issuecomment-2716125817](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11122#issuecomment-2716125817)
        1. Consensus in the room that this is the right direction.
    1. [smaug] Should we try (again) to remove XSLT? (Move to April 10)
        1. Some usage numbers: [XSLTProcessor](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/79), [XSLProcessingInstruction](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/78)
        1. There are at least [some](https://github.com/DesignLiquido/xslt-processor) JS implementations
        1. There are some concerns about the accuracy of the usage data we can collect. We will revisit this topic on April 10.
    1. [Luke] [File upload control rendering should specify the button element to use](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11130)
        1. Luke will create a PR to specify that it is a button.
    1. [Emilio] [Clarify correct behavior for requestAnimationFrame for hidden iframes (display: none)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11138)
        1. Mason will ping Chris for his opinion. We'd like WebKit's opinion on their appetite around the compat risk here.
1. New topics
    1. [Simon] [History API: PushState can silently fail in Chromium while Gecko/Webkit raises exception](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11108)
        1. Consensus is that Chromium will change their behavior and Simon will write a spec PR to formalize this.

### Action Items

1. @lukewarlow will create a PR for [file upload control rendering should specify the button element to use](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11130) to specify that it is a button.
1. @mfreed7 will ping Chris for his opinion on [clarify correct behavior for requestAnimationFrame for hidden iframes (display: none)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11138).
1. @zcorpan will write a spec PR to formalize exception throwing for [History API: PushState can silently fail in Chromium while Gecko/Webkit raises exception](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11108).

### Minutes  
panos: reviewing prior action items. Anything new from Olli/Anne on ARIA notify? Sounds like no.  
panos: native/primitive appearance?   
joey: there's an issue in CSSWG about native appearance (generally), nothing specific to `<select>`. There are open questions there for Anne.  
stephen: hasn't come up. One issue proposed for async resolution.  
mason: that's the :hover style algorithm w.r.t. top layer elements.  
stephen: There's also a CSSWG F2F next week - that would be a good time.  
panos: last prior action item: dialog open attribute. Any comments? Sound like no - keep on the list.  
panos: carryovers. Naming of composed range.  
di: started discussion last time. Adding a new definition of range where endpoints are composed (cross shadow trees). Deciding on the naming. We already agreed that the existing range is "legacy uncomposed range". What should the composed range be called? Composed range? Composed selection range?  
simon: olli isn't here, but he didn't like "legacy", because it isn't legacy, it is supported. I don't have strong opinions otherwise.  
di: anne had very strong opinions about "legacy" and olli had weak objections.  
dom: any disagreement on how to move forward? It's just naming.  
di: seems ok to me. But I do need to clarify the composed range naming.  
dom: did anne or olli express opinions there?  
di: no opinions that I've heard yet.  
emilio: why "selection"? You can use them for non-selection things.  
di: at first we called it "legacy selection range", and wanted to keep "selection".  
emilio: maybe "composed range" and "uncomposed range"?  
dom: the composed range is only used by selection API, so we're trying to make it explicit.  
emilio: you could do custom highlights with composed ranges eventually, right?  
dom: the only way you get access to composed range is through selection API  
emilio: that's just for now, but who knows later?  
dan: I agree with emilio. I'm surprised to not see "composed range" and "same tree range". "Legacy" shouts to not use this. This is just describing spec terms, not impl, so not strong opinions.  
mason: I agree, composed range and uncomposed range tells me what they are. But it's all spec terms anyway, let's just agree on something.  
emilio: "same tree range" feels odd.   
stephen: +1 someone has already raised an issue about highlights and shadow roots, so there's a use case.  
dom: Let's remove "selection" from the name, and hash it out on the issue. Thanks for the feedback.  
panos: did everyone agree to remove "legacy"?  
dom: I heard agreement about that, let's see what happens on the issue.  
panos: ok, updated the consensus from the room in the notes, and people can chime in.  
panos: next issue: FACE reset algorithm.  
dom: anne wanted to discuss, so maybe not good to discuss. Idea: custom element is created and appended to the DOM by the parser, the form reset algorithm is called, unless it's a custom element. That's the only piece of the reset algorithm that isn't called by any browser in any instance.  
dom: we could update the spec/WPTs to match browsers, or change behavior. Anne said this deviates from the idea that custom elements explain elements. But it feels like changing behavior is a big lift.  
mason: are there developers with strong opinions?  
dom: no, it just seems like complaint that the spec doesn't match the behavior  
dan: unless someone is pushing for a big change, it sounds right to modify the spec.  
dom: I don't know of anyone pushing for it. I'll update the spec PR and land it.  
panos: anne basically sounded like he wanted discussion, which we just did. Good.  
panos: next item, removing XSLT. There are usage numbers.  
stephen: I have concerns. I kept this up to date historically for Chromium, and I don't trust the use counters based on my experience. Total usage might be higher.  
dan: even if the data were accurate, not enough zeros for the usage to be low enough.  
mason: is XSLT supported officially?  
simon: supported  
mason: maybe we could just mark it deprecated in the spec, to make the statement that we're not actively working on it.  
brian: we could do that on MDN too. This would be the first time we have something baseline widely available that we've marked as removed.  
dan: maybe we could offer helpful pointers to alternatives that are better, and why they're better.  
panos: maybe a question for olli. But I like brian's suggestion to mark it in all the places.  
dan: it won't go far unless developers know what to use instead.  
brian: talk about it in those terms also. Would anyone want to come on the podcast and talk about it? I'm guessing people will have objections.  
emilio: we have a history of security bugs, etc.  
stephen: yeah that was a big deal  
mason: yeah we get bugs about it and have to basically ignore them, which sucks  
brian: people do use it and some like it  
panos: put a pin in it, and talk with olli next time?  
panos: next thing is file upload control rendering  
luke: I'm implementing details content - element backed pseudo. And the file upload is spec'd that way but isn't implemented that way. If browsers do that, there will be interop issues. WebKit/Blink use input button, vs. Gecko which uses a real button. input buttons are replaced, so pseudos are different.  
luke: should we specify that it's a real button? spec says it uses button "layout" but not the actual element under the covers. CSS spec says it should be a `<button>`. there has been pushback from anne - should we be requiring stuff for appearance:auto? fair. This is a special case. Opinions?  
simon: input type=file is interesting because it doesn't use appearance itself.  
emilio: the appearance applies to the button but not the element. Just make it a button, I agree. When I wrote the spec, this wasn't observable, but then people made pseudos and it technically is observable.  
mason: any impl or compat changes?  
emilio: shouldn't be, no. Easy change. Element backed pseudo element - seems better to use button  
mason: when appearance:base comes around, it might matter?  
luke: not a compat issue, not an impl issue. Already patched in Blink. Seems straightforward. Just need to decide. Feels best to just say it's a real button. Technically optional to have a button even.  
joey: I agree, let's use a real button. But if Anne disagrees, maybe we can achieve interop in other ways.  
luke: alternative is to say it's not element-backed, especially in appearance:base mode. Hard to make it switch based on appearance.  
emilio: should this be in HTML at all? we're having a css-forms-1 discussion, wherever we define appearance:base stuff is where the tree of controls should live. And as Simon says, appearance:auto doesn't apply to file.  
luke: I'll make a PR to say it's a button. And we can see if Anne has objections.  
emilio: this is low hanging fruit. Hopefully no objections, since there's no impl concern or anything. In appearance:auto mode, maybe you want to do something more native/fancy and don't expose it, but that doesn't apply here.  
luke: ok, thanks. Will change it.  
panos: next thing is correct behavior for rAF.  
emilio: spec allows both behaviors, which isn't great. There's an interop difference, firefox won't fire rAF for display:none frames. I suspect we fire other events in this case, like IO. I'm looking into this stuff, so I'm willing to fix it to match the spec. Big question: is there a known reason webkit/blink fire on display:none frames? Are people willing to converge to one behavior? My preference would be to not fire them. Is there a reason?  
mason: Do people do this? Compat?  
emilio: not that I'm aware of. Weird that display:none fires, but removing the iframe doesn't.  
panos: maybe wait for webkit folks?  
emilio: sure. We can't just change it blindly, but a general question is whether we can try to change it.  
mason: I can ping Chris to see if he has opinions. (done)  
panos: next item is the history question.  
simon: this is an interop question. Exception being thrown or not.  
dom: I spoke to Noam about this, and we're willing to change behavior, if mozilla is willing to update the spec.  
noam: the reason I was mildly objecting is that it's an old API, and would mostly affect existing sites, especially since navigation is in interop. This is about changing an legacy API that mostly affects existing sites, which maybe aren't being maintained. Of course, it currently throws in firefox/safari so it would be on blink-only sites. We'd just be adding throw behaviors for existing users, not helping new developers. But this is a weak objection.  
simon: ok thanks.  
emilio: is the rate limit consistent across browsers?  
dom: doesn't have to be, per spec, and I don't know about behavior.  
emilio: I think throwing is better behavior. It's a bit weird for something to throw in one browser and not another. Edge case situation though.  
dom: two browsers do it, and it's an edge case, maybe concerns are small. But there is a compat concern. Perhaps not strong enough to stop this.  
emilio: I agree, it doesn't sound risky. Idea behind the limit is preventing malicious actors. Real sites shouldn't hit this limit, right? Other than page bugs, etc. Ideally we aim for interop, especially for throwing exceptions. Limit in chromium is 100, firefox is 90, likely doesn't matter.  
dom: disparity in limits already exist  
noam: You reach this limit when you have a bug, and you do pushstate on the `input` handler for the slider, and you add a ton of stuff to the history. Etc. Likely a bug during development.  
emilio: fairly unlikely to cause real issues if you start throwing, and perhaps better.  
noam: but some sites might have shipped this bug, and they'll start throwing.  
emilio: but those are already broken in firefox/safari. Not a hill to die on.  
dom: it's more complicated, there are rate limiters, etc. Nuanced enough to not have valid use cases that trip it.  
dom: ok resolved then.  
panos: who from chromium can drive this behavior change?  
dom: I don't know when, but we can commit to doing it.  
simon: I can write a spec PR.  
panos: great, agreed.  
panos: anything else to discuss?
